title: Izalontamab Brengitecan in Locally Advanced or Metastatic Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer With Actionable Genomic Alterations Outside of Classical EGFR Mutations: A Phase Ib Study
author: Huaqiang Zhou; Hongyun Zhao; Xue Hou; Yongsheng Wang; Zhiyong He; Yongsheng Li; Yuxiang Ma; Yuanyuan Zhao; Yan Huang; Likun Chen; Sa Xiao; Hai Zhu; Yi Zhu; Wenfeng Fang; Li Zhang; Yunpeng Yang
text:
Abstract
PURPOSE
To evaluate the safety and efficacy of izalontamab brengitecan (iza-bren) in patients with non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring actionable genomic alterations (GAs) outside of classical epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations.
METHODS
Eligible patients had locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with prespecific actionable GAs, had progressed after standard treatment and received no more than one previous line of chemotherapy. iza-bren was administered at the dose of 2.5 mg/kg once per day on days 1 and 8 of each 3-week cycle. The primary end point was safety. The secondary end points included objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), and duration of response. The exploratory end points included progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS).
RESULTS
A total of 83 patients with NSCLC were enrolled in four cohorts: EGFR exon20ins/nonclassical mutations (n = 14), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) mutation (n = 19), KRAS/BRAF/MET mutation (n = 26), and ALK/ROS1/RET/NTRK fusion (n = 24). The most common grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were thrombocytopenia (51.8%), anemia (44.6%), and neutropenia (43.4%). The most frequent nonhematologic TRAEs of all grades were nausea (49.4%), asthenia (45.8%), stomatitis (44.6%), and diarrhea (38.6%). One case of grade 2 interstitial lung disease was observed. The confirmed ORR was 39.7%, and the DCR was 85.9%. The median PFS was 7.0 months (95% CIs, 5.4 to 10.5), while OS data were immature. Patients with EGFR exon20ins or other nonclassical mutations achieved an ORR of 69.2% with a median PFS of 10.5 months (95% CI, 6.9 to not reached); the HER2-mutant cohort had an ORR of 52.9% and a median PFS of 7.5 months (95% CI, 5.4 to not reached).
CONCLUSION
iza-bren demonstrated encouraging antitumor activity and a manageable safety profile in pretreated NSCLC patients with diverse GAs outside of classical EGFR mutations, especially in EGFR exon20ins/nonclassical and HER2 mutations.
INTRODUCTION
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), accounting for approximately 85% of cases.1,2 Advances in the molecular characterization of NSCLC have revealed a complex landscape of genomic alterations (GAs), which have enabled the development of targeted therapies for specific patient populations.3,4 Among these, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations occur in 15% to 50% of patients, depending on ethnicity; KRAS mutations in approximately 30%, and ALK rearrangements in 3% to 7%. Other actionable alterations—including ROS1, BRAF, NTRK, MET, RET, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)—collectively represent an additional 15% to 20% of NSCLC cases.5,6 Although tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have substantially improved outcomes for patients with targetable alterations, resistance invariably develops, leaving limited subsequent treatment options.7 Furthermore, for some driver mutations, such as non-G12C KRAS mutations, effective targeted agents have yet to be developed.8 This therapeutic landscape underscores a critical unmet need for novel treatment strategies.
CONTEXT
Key Objective
To evaluate the safety and preliminary efficacy of izalontamab brengitecan (iza-bren) in patients with non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring actionable genomic alterations outside of classical epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations.
Knowledge Generated
iza-bren demonstrated an objective response rate (ORR) of 39.7% across the overall cohort. Particularly strong activity was observed in patients with EGFR exon20 insertions or other uncommon EGFR mutations (ORR 69.2%) or human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) mutations (52.9%). The safety profile was manageable.
Relevance (T.E. Stinchcombe)
Based on these preliminary results, additional trials in patients with NSCLC with EGFR exon20 insertion mutations, nonclassical EGFR mutations, and HER2 mutations are warranted.*
*Relevance section written by JCO Associate Editor Thomas E. Stinchcombe, MD.
Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) represent a rapidly emerging transformative class of anticancer agents and have shown clinical benefit in NSCLC with HER2 or EGFR mutations.9-14 Despite these milestones, the therapeutic potential of ADCs in patients harboring other uncommon actionable GAs is still in the early stages. Monospecific ADCs such as Dato-DXd and patritumab deruxtecan have initially shown broad clinical activity in patients with nonclassical EGFR mutations, providing a proof-of-concept for this modality.15,16
Izalontamab brengitecan (iza-bren, BL-B01D1) is a novel, first-in-class bispecific ADC simultaneously targeting both EGFR and HER3. This agent consists of an anti-EGFR human IgG1 antibody fused to two anti-HER3 single-chain variable fragments, conjugated via a cleavable linker to Ed-04, a potent topoisomerase I inhibitor with a drug-to-antibody ratio of 8. iza-bren is expected to have a dual target effect, disrupting the core oncogenic signaling in ERBB family. For tumors driven by other oncogenes (eg, KRAS, BRAF), it is hypothesized that these tumors maintain a partial dependency on the EGFR/ERBB signaling pathway for survival and proliferation.17 It may effectively overcome the drug resistance caused by the tumor antigens heterogeneity. In a first-in-human phase I trial we reported, iza-bren demonstrated a manageable safety profile and promising antitumor activity in heavily pretreated solid tumors.18 iza-bren 2.5 mg/kg once per day on days 1 and 8 of each 3-week cycle was selected in this study as the recommended phase II dose (RP2D) in Chinese patients.
This study aimed to evaluate the safety and antitumor activity of iza-bren in patients with NSCLC harboring actionable GAs outside of classical TKI-sensitizing EGFR mutations.
METHODS
Study Design and Participants
BL-B01D1-101 (China Drug Trials, CTR20212923, and ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05194982) is a first-in-human, open-label, multicenter, dose-escalation and dose-expansion, phase Ia/Ib study evaluating iza-bren monotherapy in patients with locally advanced or metastatic solid tumors. The study design is shown in the Data Supplement (Fig S1, online only). In this paper, we report a cohort analysis in patients with NSCLC harboring actionable GAs outside of classical EGFR mutations from the dose-expansion part. This cohort analysis was prespecified when designing the phase Ib study and had been planned to be conducted after the completion of comprehensive safety and efficacy reviews of accumulated data.
Key inclusion criteria were age 18 years or older; histologically or cytologically confirmed locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC (squamous or nonsquamous); the presence of prespecified actionable GAs other than common EGFR exon 19 deletions or L858R mutation (including EGFR exon 20 insertions, or other nonclassical EGFR mutations [eg, G719X, S768I, L861Q], HER2 mutations, KRAS, BRAF [V600E or non-V600E mutations]), or MET mutations (MET exon 14 skipping mutation), or ALK, ROS1, or RET fusion, testing locally; measurable disease per RECIST, version 1.1; an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status score of 0 or 1; and adequate organ function. The full inclusion and exclusion criteria are provided in the Protocol (online only).
Eligible patients had disease progression after previous standard therapy per Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO) Guidelines on Diagnosis and Treatment of Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer (only up to one previous line of systemic chemotherapy was allowed).
Treatment
Patients received iza-bren intravenously at 2.5 mg/kg once per day on days 1 and 8 of every 3-week cycle (dose compensated per study protocol). Treatment continued until disease progression per RECIST version 1.1, unacceptable toxicities, withdrawal of consent, initiation of new anticancer treatment, or investigator decision.
End Points
The primary end point was safety. Adverse events were defined and graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (NCI-CTCAE) v5.0. The secondary end points included objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), and duration of response (DOR). Tumor response was evaluated by local investigators according to RECIST version 1.1. Exploratory end points included progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS).
Assessments
Safety monitoring continued throughout the study, extending until 28 days after the last dose or initiation of other antitumor treatment. Radiologic tumor assessments by using enhanced computed tomography or enhanced magnetic resonance imaging were performed at baseline, every 6 weeks during the first year of treatment, and every 12 weeks thereafter. Baseline scans included neck, chest, abdomen (including bilateral adrenal glands and pelvis), and brain. Subsequent scans during treatment were performed for tumor sites, and the imaging technique was the same with that used at baseline.
Statistical Analysis
Safety data were summarized descriptively. ORR and DCR were calculated with corresponding two-sided 95% CIs using the Clopper-Pearson method. Kaplan-Meier methods were used to estimate time-to-event outcomes, including PFS, OS, and DOR. Median values were reported and their 95% CIs were calculated using the Brookmeyer-Crowley method. For DOR and PFS, a patient was censored if no radiologic progressive disease and death were reported before the data cutoff date (March 28, 2025). For OS, a patient was censored if no death was reported before the data cutoff date. The median follow-up time was computed using the reverse Kaplan-Meier method. Subgroup analyses were prespecified for patients with EGFR exon20 insertions, other nonclassical EGFR mutations, HER2 mutations, and KRAS/BRAF/MET mutations. All statistical analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 or higher (SAS Institute, Cary, NC).
Trial Oversight
The study was approved by the institutional review board at each participating site and conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. All patients provided written consent.
RESULTS
Between August 25, 2023, and March 28, 2025, a total of 83 patients were enrolled across five centers in China and received at least one dose of izalontamab brengitecan (iza-bren; Data Supplement, Table S1). At data cutoff, 39 patients remained on treatment. Treatment discontinuation occurred in 44 (53.0%) patients due to disease progression (35 [42.2%]), adverse events (3 [3.6%]; two due to treatment-related AEs), patient withdrawal (4 [4.8%]), and other reasons (2 [2.4%]; Fig 1).
Baseline demographics and disease characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The median age was 57.0 years (range, 28-78), 34 (41%) patients were female, and 7 (8.4%) had brain metastases. A total of 67.5% of patients had received one line of previous therapy, while 32.5% had received two or more. Additionally, 50.6% of patients had previously received anti–PD-1/anti–PD-L1 immunotherapy. Among the seven patients with EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations, six (85.7%) had received first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. For patients with HER2 mutations, all had received previous chemotherapy, while a subset had been treated with HER2-directed agents (two with a HER2-ADC and three with a HER2-TKI). Two patients with KRAS G12C mutations had been treated with KRAS G12C inhibitors. Consistent with established guidelines, most patients with other actionable alterations—including those with nonclassical EGFR mutations (6/7, 85.7%), BRAF V600E mutations (100%), MET exon 14 skipping alterations (100%), and ALK fusion (100%), RET fusion (4/5, 80%), ROS1 fusion (100%), or NTRK fusion (100%)—had received a corresponding targeted therapy before enrollment (Data Supplement, Tables S2 and S3). The only exceptions were two individuals: one patient with a nonclassical EGFR mutation and one with a RET fusion, both of whom had received chemotherapy only.

Safety
All 83 patients were evaluable for safety. The median duration of drug exposure was 4.1 months (range, 0.03-17.7). All patients (100%) experienced treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs; as assessed by investigator) of any grade, with 66 (79.5%) experiencing grade ≥3 events (Table 2). TRAEs led to dose reduction in 46 (55.4%) patients and drug delay in 44 (53.0%) patients (Data Supplement, Table S4). The most common TRAEs leading to dose reductions were thrombocytopenia (n = 24, 28.9%), neutropenia (n = 20, 24.1%), and leukopenia (n = 13, 15.7%; Data Supplement, Table S5). Two patients discontinued iza-bren treatment due to TRAEs: asthenia, febrile neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia (Data Supplement, Table S6).

The most common TRAEs (all grades) were hematologic AEs, including anemia (88.0%), thrombocytopenia (75.9%), neutropenia (75.9%), and leukopenia (74.7%). The most frequent nonhematologic TRAEs were nausea (49.4%), asthenia (45.8%), stomatitis (44.6%), diarrhea (38.6%), and decreased appetite (34.9%; Table 2). Treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in 30 (36.1%) patients (Data Supplement, Table S4). One patient, who was previously exposed to PD-1 inhibitor, experienced grade 2 treatment-related interstitial lung disease. One patient experienced grade 1 treatment-related pneumonitis. No other case of treatment-related interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis was observed. One death (febrile neutropenia) associated with iza-bren was reported. Overall, the safety profile was manageable and no new safety signals were identified.
Efficacy
Overall Population
For the 78 patients who were included in the efficacy analyses, the median follow-up for OS was 7.3 months (95% CI, 5.5 to 9.2) and the median treatment duration was 4.1 months (range, 0.03-17.7). The ORR was 46.2% (n = 36; 95% CI, 34.8 to 57.8), which comprised 31 confirmed partial responses (cPR) and five partial responses pending confirmation. Tumor responses were observed across various mutation types (Table 3; Fig 2). The DCR was 85.9% (n = 67; 95% CI, 76.2 to 92.7). Best change from baseline in target lesion size is shown in Figure 2A. Changes in tumor burden over time are shown in Figure 2B. Responses to iza-bren were durable; at a median follow-up of 6.9 months, the median duration of response was not reached (NR; 95% CI, 5.7 to NR). At a median follow-up of 8.2 months, the median PFS was 7.0 months (95% CI, 5.4 to 10.5; Data Supplement, Fig S2). Overall survival data were not mature, with only 11 (14.1%) overall survival events (deaths) observed as of data cutoff (Data Supplement, Fig S3).

Prespecified Subgroups
In patients harboring EGFR exon 20 insertions or other nonclassical EGFR mutations, the ORR and confirmed ORR were 69.2% (n = 9; Table 3), with a median PFS of 10.5 months (Data Supplement, Fig S2). Among patients with EGFR exon 20 insertions, 85.7% (six of seven) achieved cPR (Data Supplement, Fig S4). In the HER2-mutant cohort, the ORR and confirmed ORR were 52.9% (n = 9), with a median PFS of 7.5 months (Table 3, Data Supplement, Fig S2).
In patients harboring KRAS/BRAF/MET mutation, the ORR was 40.0% (n = 10; 95% CI, 21.1 to 61.3; Table 3), with a median PFS of 7.0 months (95% CI, 3.0 to NR; Data Supplement, Fig S2). Within this group, among the eight patients with KRAS G12C mutations, four patients achieved cPR.
In patients harboring ALK/ROS1/RET fusion, the ORR was 34.8% (n = 8; 95% CI, 16.4 to 57.3), with a median PFS of 3.8 months (95% CI, 2.7 to 4.8; Table 3, Data Supplement, Fig S2). Responses in this group were observed in patients with ALK (n = 3), ROS1 (n = 3), and RET (n = 2) fusions.
Antitumor activity by all GA types is presented in the Data Supplement (Table S8).
DISCUSSION
In this phase Ib study, iza-bren, a first-in-class bispecific ADC targeting EGFR and HER3, demonstrated encouraging antitumor activity and a manageable safety profile in patients with advanced NSCLC harboring diverse actionable GAs outside of classical EGFR mutations. iza-bren showed an ORR of 46.2%, with particularly promising activity observed in the subgroup with ERBB family alterations (EGFR exon20ins, other nonclassical mutations, and HER2 mutations) and in those with KRAS G12C mutation. The safety profile was consistent with the previous phase Ia report, with no new safety signals identified. To our knowledge, this is the first trial to show clinically meaningful activity of a bispecific ADC in this genetically heterogeneous and therapeutically underserved population.
Although targeted therapies are available for many of these GAs, such as nonclassical EGFR mutations, HER2 mutations, or KRAS, BRAF, C-MET, and ALK/ROS1/RET fusions, resistance is inevitable, and usually these patients often derive limited benefit from immunotherapy.19-21 Consequently, chemotherapy frequently serves as the treatment backbone for these patients after the failure of targeted therapies, and both ORR and PFS are very limited.22 In this trial, iza-bren achieved a confirmed objective response rate of 39.7% and a median progression-free survival of 7.0 months across the overall cohort. Importantly, patients with EGFR exon20 insertions or other uncommon EGFR mutations derived the greatest benefit, with confirmed ORR of 69.2% and median progression-free survival of 10.5 months. These findings highlight the potential of iza-bren to address a critical unmet need in this patient population.
Although these results are highly encouraging, it is crucial to acknowledge that the landscape of lung cancer treatment is rapidly evolving and some patients remain naïve to recently launched targeted agents. For patients with EGFR exon20ins mutations, the treatment landscape has been transformed by the PAPILLON trial, which established the combination of amivantamab with chemotherapy as a (US) Food and Drug Administration–approved, NCCN-recommended preferred first-line option.23 For patients who failed the first-line chemotherapy, established second-line therapies include single-agent amivantamab (if not used previously) and sunvozertinib, which have demonstrated ORR of 40% and 61%, respectively.24,25 In our study, most patients (6/7) had received previous platinum-based chemotherapy but not the above-mentioned targeted therapy. From this perspective, iza-bren achieved a confirmed ORR of 85.7%, which is comparable with amivantamab and sunvozertinib in the second-line setting. However, the efficacy of iza-bren in patients who have progressed on amivantamab or sunvozertinib represents a critical unanswered question and a key area for future investigation. Similarly, for patients with HER2-mutant NSCLC, T-DXd and zongertinib is the standard of care for subsequent therapy.11,26 In the DESTINY-Lung02 trial, T-DXd demonstrated an ORR of 55%.11 In our study, only a minority of patients (5 of 19) had received a previous HER2-directed therapy. iza-bren achieved a confirmed ORR of 52.9%, which is similar to the efficacy of T-DXd in a population resistant to chemotherapy. But the efficacy of iza-bren among patients previously treated with platinum-based chemotherapy and a HER2-targeted ADC/TKI remained unknown. The treatment sequence for iza-bren is a question for the future.
Our results build on recent advances with ADCs in NSCLC.27 Trastuzumab deruxtecan has shown durable activity in HER2-mutant disease, and TROP2-directed ADCs have recently entered clinical practice for patients progressing on EGFR-TKIs.10,13-15 Furthermore, Dato-DXd and patritumab deruxtecan have initially shown broad clinical activity across NSCLC, including in patients with nonclassical GAs.15,16 The bispecific design of iza-bren, targeting both EGFR and HER3, may enhance tumor selectivity and overcome resistance mechanisms associated with HER family signaling.18,28-30 The antitumor activity observed across multiple subgroups—including EGFR exon20 insertions, HER2 mutations, and KRAS/BRAF/MET alterations—suggests that iza-bren has a unique therapeutic scope beyond currently available ADCs. This superior response is likely attributable to the dual impact of the antibody component on both drug selectivity and receptor internalization.
By contrast, iza-bren demonstrated more modest efficacy in patients with ALK rearrangements (ORR, 23.1%). This observation is not unique to iza-bren and aligns with other ADC trials. For instance, in the TROPION-Lung05 study, Dato-DXd also achieved a limited ORR of 23.5% in heavily pretreated patients with ALK rearrangements.15 Compared with other GA types, patients with ALK/ROS1/RET/NTRK fusions were heavily pretreated, with 11 (45.8%) patients previously treated with ≥3 lines of therapy, which may be a contributing factor for the lower ORR. Elucidating the precise mechanisms behind this observation is critical and warrants further biomarker research.
The safety profile of iza-bren observed in this study was consistent with our previously published phase Ia data, with no new safety signals identified.18 The most frequent grade ≥3 TRAEs were hematologic, including anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and leukopenia. These events were efficiently managed with standard supportive care and dose reduction. The effective management of these events is underscored by the low rate of treatment discontinuation due to TRAEs, which was only 2.3%. Because the dose of the antibody (izalontamab) is low, the classical EGFR inhibitor–related toxicities were mostly grade 1 or 2 (grade ≥3 stomatitis, 3.6%; grade ≥3 diarrhea, 7.2%). Interstitial lung disease is a notable risk associated with several ADCs. For example, T-Dxd has reported all-grade ILD rates of 9.7%-12.9% in advanced NSCLC, with grade≥3 events occurring in 1.4%-2.0% of patients. By contrast, only one case (1.4%) of grade 2 ILD was observed in our study, indicating a relatively low risk with iza-bren.
Our study had several limitations. First, as a phase Ib study, the sample size was relatively small, and subgroups consisted of a limited number of patients exclusively in China. Therefore, the results should be interpreted with caution. The reported response rates are descriptive, in keeping with the exploratory nature of a phase I study. Findings need to be explored in multinational larger cohort. Second, the single-arm, nonrandomized nature of the trial precludes direct comparison with standard therapies and introduces the potential for selection bias. Third, the follow-up duration remains relatively short, and long-term survival outcomes could not be fully characterized. Fourth, the study relied on genomic profiling from local laboratories and tumor assessments by local investigators. Fifth, as highlighted, the treatment landscape for NSCLC has evolved rapidly. This impacts the generalizability of our findings and underscores the urgent need for future studies to define the treatment sequence of iza-bren. Finally, the low incidence of baseline brain metastases in our study may limit the generalizability of our findings to a broader, population with brain metastases.
In conclusion, iza-bren demonstrated robust antitumor activity in pretreated NSCLC patients with diverse GAs outside of classical EGFR mutations, especially in EGFR exon20ins/nonclassical and HER2 mutations. The most common adverse events associated with iza-bren are hematologic toxicities, which were generally manageable, with no new safety signals observed.
